title: The Normal Distribution
objectives: Standardise any normal variable to a standard normal via z = (x, mu)/sigma
Compute normal probabilities using stated table values for the standard normal CDF
Apply the 68-95-99.7 rule for quick distribution statements
Compute a parametric Value at Risk from a normal model and articulate its tail-risk caveat
motivation: Ask a risk system for a 95% confidence number and it will hand you a z-value of 1.645, a fact about the normal distribution. The normal is the workhorse curve of quantitative finance: sums of many small effects (the central limit theorem) look normal, and almost every closed-form risk or pricing formula assumes it. Learning to standardise and read normal probabilities is the single most reusable calculation skill in this curriculum.

blocks.md: The **normal distribution** $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has the famous symmetric bell shape: centred at the mean $\mu$, with the standard deviation $\sigma$ controlling the width. Symmetry means the mean, median and mode all coincide at $\mu$; about 68% of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three, the **68-95-99.7 rule**. Different $(\mu, \sigma)$ just relocate and rescale the same shape, which motivates the standardisation step below.

blocks.caption: Normal density and standardisation to a standard normal Z

blocks.md: Every normal variable reduces to the **standard normal** $Z$ by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, the $z$-score measures distance from the mean in units of $\sigma$. Because $z$ is dimensionless, one table of its cumulative distribution $\Phi(z)$ serves every normal problem in existence. Why the normal is everywhere: the central limit theorem says averages and sums of many small independent effects end up normal, whatever the underlying ingredients, which is why short-horizon returns, measurement noise and forecasting errors all wear this shape as a first approximation.

A notational trap deserves its own paragraph: statisticians write $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with the **variance** as the second argument, while many software packages expect the standard deviation, passing 0.01 to a function that wants a variance is a hundredfold error. In this curriculum the second argument is always a variance, and quantities are stated in units: a "1% daily volatility" is $\sigma = 0.01$, a variance of $0.0001$. Writing down which convention you are using before computing is a two-second habit that prevents the most embarrassing class of risk-report errors.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a probability from the table
items: IQ-style scores: $X \sim N(100, 15^2)$. Probability of scoring 130 or more: $z = (130 - 100)/15 = 2.0$.
Table: $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$, so $P(X \ge 130) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228$ - about 2.3%, or roughly 1 person in 44.
Returns version: with $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 1\%$ daily, a -2% day has $z = -2$, and by symmetry $P(R \le -2\%) = 1 - \Phi(2) \approx 0.0228$.
Same arithmetic everywhere: convert to $z$, read $\Phi$, flip with $1 - \Phi$ for right tails.

blocks.caption: The standard normal: shaded area between -1 and 1 is about 68%; move mu and sigma and notice only the axis labels change, never the shape.

blocks.text: Value at Risk in one line

blocks.md: **Value at Risk (VaR)** answers: "how bad is a bad day?" Formally it is a quantile of the loss distribution, the threshold that losses exceed with probability $\alpha$. With a normal model for daily PnL (mean $\mu$, volatility $\sigma$) the parametric VaR collapses to one multiplication:

blocks.title: Worked example: 95% one-day VaR
items: Portfolio worth \$1,000,000; daily mean return $\mu \approx 0$; daily volatility $\sigma = 1\%$.
95% VaR uses the 95th normal percentile: $z_{0.95} = 1.645$ (from the table above).
Statement: on about 5 days in 100, we expect to lose more than \$16,450. At 99% confidence, $z = 2.33$ gives \$23,300.

blocks.title: The normal model lies in the tails
blocks.md: Real daily returns have **fat tails**: extreme moves are far more frequent than the normal predicts. A -22% day (October 1987) is a 20-plus sigma event under a 1%-volatility normal model, normal maths calls it impossible, markets called it a Monday. Treat normal VaR as a transparent baseline, check it against simulated or historical quantiles, and expect the 99%+ numbers to be too optimistic. Later lessons give you the t-distribution for heavier tails.

blocks.code:
from math import erf, sqrt

phi = lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))  # standard normal CDF
print(round(phi(-2), 4))            # P(Z <= -2), left tail
print(round(1 - phi(2), 4))         # symmetry: identical right tail

var95 = 1.645 * 0.01 * 1_000_000
print(f"{var95:,.0f}")              # 95% one-day VaR in dollars
blocks.caption: The erf-based standard normal CDF reproduces the table values to four decimals.

guidedExercise.prompt: Weekly PnL of a strategy is modelled as $N(0, 8^2)$ in thousands of dollars (so $\sigma = \$8{,}000$). Compute $P(\text{PnL} > 12{,}000)$ using a stated table value, and the 95% VaR of the weekly PnL.
hints: The 95% quantile of the standard normal is 1.645.
guidedExercise.solution: $z = 12/8 = 1.5$; the table gives $\Phi(1.5) \approx 0.9332$, so $P(\text{PnL} > 12{,}000) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668$ (about 6.7%). VaR: $1.645 \times 8{,}000 = \$13{,}160$, losses beyond that occur about 5% of weeks.

independentExercise.prompt: A \$5,000,000 fixed-income book has daily volatility 0.8% and negligible mean. Compute the 99% one-day VaR using $z_{0.99} = 2.33$. Then compute how many sigmas a -\$120,000 day represents, and whether the normal model would call it surprising.
hints: Convert the dollar loss into a return first: divide by the book size.
independentExercise.solution: VaR $= 2.33 \times 0.008 \times 5{,}000{,}000 = \$93{,}200$. A -\$120,000 day is a return of $-120{,}000/5{,}000{,}000 = -2.4\%$, i.e. $z = -2.4/0.8 = -3.0$ sigmas. Under the normal model a 3-sigma day has probability about 0.13%, roughly once in two years of trading days, so it would be flagged as a rare surprise. (In real markets such days arrive more often; that is the fat-tail caveat.)

commonMistakes: Forgetting to standardise: reading P(X >= 130) directly from the table as if X were already Z.
Using 1.645 for a two-sided 95% interval, two-sided needs 1.96 on each side (2.5% in each tail).
Applying the 68-95-99.7 rule asymmetrically, it applies to |X, mu|, both tails at once.
Trusting normal VaR at 99%+ confidence, where fat tails in real returns make the model most wrong.
realWorldApplication: Measurement errors, test scores and industrial tolerances are quoted with normal-based confidence statements; z-scores are the universal language for 'how unusual is this observation?' in any field that averages things.
quantFinanceApplication: Parametric VaR is the z-quantile times the portfolio volatility, the \$16,450 worked example is exactly how a risk engine turns \$1,000,000 notional and 1% daily volatility into a one-number risk limit, and regulatory capital calculations use the same standardisation machinery.
summary: $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is fully described by mean and standard deviation; all probabilities come from standardising $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ and reading $\Phi$.
68-95-99.7: mass within 1, 2, 3 standard deviations of the mean.
Parametric VaR = $z_{\alpha} \times \sigma \times \text{value}$: one multiplication from vol to a dollar risk limit.
The normal is the CLT's baseline shape, but real return tails are fatter, trust it in the middle, doubt it at the extremes.

quiz.prompt: $X \sim N(100, 15^2)$. What is $P(X \ge 130)$, using $\Phi(2) = 0.9772$? (4 decimal places.)
For a normal distribution, roughly what fraction of observations lies **within two standard deviations** of the mean?
quiz.explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% within one sigma, 95% within two, 99.7% within three.

quiz.prompt: A \$1,000,000 portfolio has daily volatility 1% and negligible mean. Using $z_{0.95} = 1.645$, what is the 95% one-day VaR in dollars?
What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
from math import erf, sqrt
phi = lambda z: 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))
print(round(phi(-2), 4))
print(round(1 - phi(2), 4))
quiz.explanation: The standard normal is symmetric: $\Phi(-2) = 1 - \Phi(2)$, and both equal about 0.0228.

quiz.prompt: Which is the most important caveat when reporting a 99% parametric (normal) VaR?
options: Real return distributions have fat tails, so losses beyond VaR occur more often than 1% and are more severe than the model suggests
It cannot be computed without Monte Carlo simulation
It ignores the portfolio's expected return entirely
quiz.explanation: The normal underestimates tail frequency and severity, the 1987 crash was a 20-sigma event under normal maths. The mean's absence is a minor issue at short horizons; units and computability are non-issues.

quiz.prompt: Why does one standard normal table serve every normal distribution?
quiz.modelAnswer: Because any normal variable can be standardised: z = (x, mu)/sigma converts N(mu, sigma^2) to N(0,1), which is dimensionless. Probabilities for any mean and scale are found by converting to z and reading the single table.
quiz.explanation: Standardisation rescales any normal to the standard normal; since the transformation is one-to-one on probability, a single table of $\Phi$ covers all $(\mu, \sigma)$ combinations.

flashcards.back: For a normal variable: ~68% of mass within 1 sigma of the mean, ~95% within 2 sigma, ~99.7% within 3 sigma.
The central limit theorem: sums and averages of many small independent effects are approximately normal, so the shape is the default first approximation for returns and errors.

flashcards.front: Spot the error: 'A -5% daily move with 1% volatility is impossible because it is a 5-sigma event.'
flashcards.back: Normal maths says a 5-sigma day has probability ~3 in 10 million, but real returns have fat tails, extreme days occur far more often than the normal predicts. 'Very unlikely' is not 'impossible'.
